definition.text: Data Privacy, as a cross-cutting concern, is keeping personally identifying content out of -- or removably out of -- every surface a run touches across the whole journey, not one redaction step. This repo's own current design already contains the sharpest version of the problem: an append-only, hash-chained ledger (F-b5-05) that must also support a data subject's right to erasure. This repo's own target architecture already proposes the shape that reconciles the two, named as its own state: a "redaction tombstone - a body removed while its digest and every proof over it still verify" -- i.e. erasing content while every existing proof over its digest keeps verifying, rather than deleting or mutating a chained row.

tools.name: FastGPT
tools.note: names per-data-class retention TTLs by environment variable (e.g. model-call traces kept six hours by default), though its own vendor disclosure admits automatic cleanup depends on background tasks that can fail. Not used by this repo.

landscape.text: The real tension in this window is architectural, not procedural: an append-only, hash-chained provenance ledger is built to make rows undeletable and unmutable, while a data-subject erasure right requires removing content on demand -- "Public permissionless ledgers are append-only by design, yet are increasingly asked to host data subject to statutory erasure obligations (GDPR Art. 17, EDPB Guidelines 02/2025)" (X-refmodel-rail-5-privacy-001). The published resolution is cryptographic erasure, not deletion: encrypt each subject's data under its own key, hash the ciphertext rather than the plaintext for chain integrity, and destroy the key to erase -- "Hash chain integrity is independent of plaintext recoverability" (X-refmodel-rail-5-privacy-008) -- a mechanism EDPB guidance itself treats as legally sufficient once the key is destroyed: "Where personal data has been encrypted using state of the art encryption technology and the encryption key has been securely destroyed, the encrypted data may be considered to have been erased, provided that decryption is not computationally feasible" (X-refmodel-rail-5-privacy-008). The closest published analogue to this repo's own agent-trace ledger applies the identical mechanism at the epoch level: "Hash chaining and Merkle batching provide tamper evidence and compact inclusion proofs," with erasure achieved by destroying epoch-key material rather than deleting log rows (X-refmodel-rail-5-privacy-003, arXiv:2609.01931) -- though that paper is explicit the mechanism is operational, not itself a legal-sufficiency finding. No adopted open standard governs the resulting erasure record: the one candidate schema, VeritasChain, 'is non-normative unless formally adopted by a recognized standards body or regulatory authority' (X-refmodel-rail-5-privacy-007), and IETF's neighboring receipt work (Vaara Receipt, ACTA signed decision receipts) is scoped to decision receipts generally, not to redaction or erasure specifically (X-refmodel-rail-5-privacy-010).

evidence.quote: Public permissionless ledgers are append-only by design, yet are increasingly asked to host data subject to statutory erasure obligations (GDPR Art. 17, EDPB Guidelines 02/2025).
Hash chaining and Merkle batching provide tamper evidence and compact inclusion proofs.
This specification is non-normative unless formally adopted by a recognized standards body or regulatory authority.

Where personal data has been encrypted using state of the art encryption technology and the encryption key has been securely destroyed, the encrypted data may be considered to have been erased, provided that decryption is not computationally feasible.

The Vaara Receipt (draft-sirkkavaara-vaara-receipt-07) specifies vaara.receipt/v1, a signed and independently recomputable record that binds a decision about an autonomous action to the evidence the decision was made on, and optionally to one or more external timestamp anchors.

usage.text: Because this spans the whole journey rather than one call, the concern is applied at three separate places, not once at intake: redaction sits in the live request path in front of every outbound model call rather than as a batch job afterward -- "production LLM redaction must sit in the live request path" (X-refmodel-rail-5-privacy-005); retention is enforced per data class with its own window rather than one blanket period, as FastGPT's own documentation names "conversation records, knowledge base files, model-call traces and audit logs" as four separately-retained classes (X-refmodel-rail-5-privacy-006); and erasure, when it reaches this repo's own hash-chained ledger, removes a body while leaving its digest and every proof over it verifying (A-state-redaction-tombstone-a-body-removed-while-its-digest-and-every-proof-over-it-still-verify) rather than deleting or editing a chained row -- a proposed design this repo has not yet built, since that same architecture entity records its own home state as absent: retention is named as something the state seam must specify and is not specified.

a body removed while its digest and every proof over it still verify
This must specify: the write model, concurrency and single-writer guarantees, the integrity mechanism, retention, and the query surface a planner needs.

gaps.what: No adopted open standard exists for a verifiable redaction/erasure record. VeritasChain, the one candidate industry schema found, calls itself non-normative unless adopted by a standards body; IETF's neighboring autonomous-decision-receipt drafts (Vaara Receipt, x402, ACTA) are not scoped to redaction or erasure. The standards array on this card is empty, and that is the honest answer, not an omission.
gaps.why_it_matters: Two implementations of 'verifiable erasure' built today would not be comparable or interoperable; the mechanism (crypto-shredding) is converging in research, but the record format that proves it happened is not.
gaps.research_query: has any standards body picked up VeritasChain's ERASURE event type, or a competing verifiable-erasure schema, since this research pass

gaps.what: This repo's own redaction-tombstone design (A-state-redaction-tombstone-...) is marked status: sourced -- the concept is grounded in F-b5-05 -- but its home_today field states plainly that it is absent: retention is named as something the state seam must specify and is not specified. Cryptographic erasure over this repo's own hash chain is a named architecture entity only -- no harness, adapter or example implements it.
gaps.why_it_matters: The corroborating academic mechanism (arXiv:2609.01931's epoch-key destruction) shows the idea is implementable, but this repo has not measured it; a claim that this repo already reconciles ledger integrity with erasure would be unevidenced.

gaps.what: The EDPB legal-sufficiency statement for crypto-shredding (record 008) was published 2026-01-18, before this research pass's own 2026-03+ recency preference, and reaches this corpus via a vendor blog restating the guideline rather than a direct fetch of EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 itself.
gaps.why_it_matters: The legal basis this card leans on for 'crypto-shredding counts as erasure' is one step removed from the regulator's own text and is dated earlier than this pass otherwise prefers; treat the attribution as flagged, not as a fetched primary source.

gaps.why_it_matters: Whether any standards body has even informally discussed a redaction/erasure event type is unconfirmed from primary text, which weakens (without refuting) the 'no adopted standard exists' finding above -- it remains the best-supported reading, but on a partial evidence base.
